chunks: Ali, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Qutayba, who said:

A man asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) a question, and he (peace be upon him) answered him regarding it. The man then said, 'What is your opinion if it were such and such — what would the ruling be regarding it?'

He (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Enough! Whatever I have answered you regarding it is from the Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family). We have nothing to do with ra'y ("what is your opinion?") regarding anything.'

key_terms.أَرَأَيْتَ: ra'y — the juristic formula for opinion-based hypothetical reasoning, rejected by the Shia Imams (AS) as a method of deriving rulings
key_terms.لَسْنَا: we are not — the Imam's collective first-person denial, on behalf of all the Ahlulbayt, of any reliance on personal opinion
key_terms.مَسْأَلَةٍ: mas'ala — a jurisprudential case or question submitted to a religious authority
key_terms.مَهْ: Mah — an interjection of sharp rebuke meaning 'enough!' or 'stop!'

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq (AS) say about the source of his rulings and why he rejected ra'y (personal opinion) in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) sharply rebuked a man who posed a hypothetical follow-up question using the juristic formula 'ara'ayta' (what is your opinion?), declaring that all his rulings trace back to the Prophet (SAWW) — not personal reasoning. This hadith is a foundational Shia creedal text rejecting ra'y (personal juristic opinion) and analogical reasoning as sources of religious law, affirming that the Imams are conduits of prophetic transmission, not independent legal reasoners.
